before.title: 5.0L AJ133 Water Pump Bearing and Seal Failure
before.description: The mechanical water pump on the 5.0L AJ133 V8 is a recognized weak point. Coolant migrates past the shaft seal into the bearing housing, corroding the bearing so the impeller shaft is no longer properly supported. This accelerates wear on the flat-face mechanical seal and lets coolant escape at the pump. Failures are common and can occur early — some owners report leaks in under 20,000 miles. Left unaddressed it leads to progressive coolant loss and overheating risk on an aluminum V8.
before.solution: Replace the water pump with the latest revised design that adds a more robust bearing and additional sealing. The current superseded OEM part number is AJ813909; Jaguar also began fitting the improved pump from the factory on later cars (XK from approx. VIN B46456). Refresh coolant and inspect the crossover/valley plastic pipe at the same time since it is the other common 5.0 cooling weak point. Typical independent-shop cost is a few hundred to well over a thousand USD depending on labor.
symptoms: Low coolant level warning message
Coolant traces around the water pump pulley/weep hole
Sweet coolant smell after driving
Coolant drips at front of engine
Rising temperature / overheating in traffic

before.title: Blocked HVAC Condensate 'Duckbill' Drain Flooding Passenger Footwell
before.description: The A/C evaporator condensate drain on the early X150 uses a rubber 'duckbill' valve (intended to keep insects out) that dries out and sticks shut over time. With the drain blocked, condensation backs up inside the HVAC box and overflows out of the housing into the front passenger footwell. Because low-mounted electronics sit in that area, prolonged water intrusion can cascade into electrical faults and module corrosion. Jaguar addressed this in TSB JTB00121 (Water Ingress into Passenger Footwell), covering XK X150 model years 2007-2009 up to a VIN break; an updated drain tube part (C2P21646) was fitted from the 2010 model year onward, which is why later 5.0L cars are far less affected.
before.solution: Clear or trim/modify the stuck duckbill drain valve on the HVAC unit and confirm free drainage; the guaranteed fix per the TSB involves dash access to replace the drain/duckbill with the updated part. Dry out the carpet/underlay, and inspect any water-affected under-dash modules. Also verify plenum/sunroof drains as a secondary water source.
symptoms: Wet or soaked passenger-side front carpet
Musty / damp smell from the vents
Water sloshing sound behind the dash
Intermittent electrical faults after wet weather

before.title: Cam (Valve) Cover Gasket Oil Leak on 4.2 AJ-V8
before.description: The 4.2 AJ-V8 cam (valve) cover gaskets harden with heat and age and begin to weep oil, often onto the exhaust manifolds (producing a burning-oil smell) and down into the spark-plug wells, where pooled oil can foul coils and cause misfires. It is a well-documented, near-universal age-related leak on these engines.
before.solution: Replace both cam-cover gaskets and the bolt grommet seals using only genuine OE parts (e.g., RH cam-cover gasket Jaguar part AJ812399) — aftermarket gaskets are widely reported to leak, and over-torquing can micro-crack the cover. Apply oil-resistant RTV only where specified. Clean oil from the plug wells and inspect coils while the covers are off.
symptoms: Oil seepage at top/sides of engine
Burning-oil smell from oil on exhaust
Oil pooling in spark-plug wells
Misfire from oil-fouled coil boots
Low oil level over time

before.title: Center Touchscreen Blank / Unresponsive (MOST-Ring Fault)
before.description: The X150's center touchscreen commonly goes black or unresponsive while audio and climate keep working, or it sticks on the Jaguar logo and never boots. The root cause is often a fault on the fiber-optic MOST network (a broken ring or a module dragging the bus down) rather than a bad screen itself. Bluetooth, DVD-navigation and Sirius modules on the ring can trigger the blackout, and weak battery/ground connections make it worse.
before.solution: First try a hard reset (disconnect battery, briefly bridge the leads) and check fuses. Diagnose the MOST fiber-optic ring to find the module breaking it (touchscreen, DVD/nav head unit, Bluetooth or Sirius module) and repair/replace that node. A used replacement touchscreen is plug-and-play with no dealer programming, and an equivalent XF-era screen interchanges with the XK.
symptoms: Black/blank touchscreen with audio still playing
Screen stuck on Jaguar logo, never reaches menu
Intermittent screen dropouts after 20+ seconds
Loss of nav/radio/Bluetooth together

before.title: Electronic Parking Brake (EPB) Motor / Module Failure
before.description: The X150 electronic parking brake is a frequent trouble spot. Small plastic serrated gears inside the EPB motor unit strip, the wiring harness between the parking brake module (PBM) and actuator chafes, and the module/switch can fault. Failures range from a 'Park Brake Fault' warning to the brake staying stuck ON so the car cannot be moved. The plastic gears are not sold separately, so a full motor assembly is usually required.
before.solution: Scan for EPB codes (e.g. C1785 motor interruption, C1799 Hall sensor circuit) and inspect the harness/connectors for chafe and corrosion before condemning parts. Repair typically means replacing the EPB motor/actuator assembly and, where present, the module — the switch is often wrongly blamed. Address a stuck-on brake promptly to avoid dragging pads and rear-caliper damage.
symptoms: 'Park Brake Fault' message / EPB warning light
Parking brake stuck on, car will not move
Grinding or motor noise from rear when applying/releasing
Beeping with EPB warning
Associated DSC / gearbox fault messages

before.title: Ignition Coil-on-Plug Misfire (Oil-Fouled Coils)
before.description: The AJ-V8 uses individual coil-on-plug ignition coils that fail with age and heat, producing single- or multi-cylinder misfires and a check-engine light. A frequent contributor is oil pooling in the spark-plug wells from a leaking cam-cover gasket, which fouls the coil boots. Coils typically last 70k-100k miles but wear faster with heavy idling and heat cycling.
before.solution: Read the misfire code to identify the cylinder, then swap the suspect coil to another cylinder to confirm the fault moves. Replace the failed coil (and spark plug); when an older high-mileage car drops one coil it is common to replace the full set and plugs together. If wells are oily, also renew the cam-cover gasket to stop recurring fouling.
symptoms: Check engine light with misfire code
Rough idle / stumble
Hesitation or loss of power under acceleration
Occasional backfire
Oil in spark-plug wells fouling coil boots

before.title: Non-Serviceable Rear Propshaft Rubber (Jurid) Coupling Splitting
before.description: The rear driveshaft (propshaft) on the X150 XK uses a bonded rubber flexible coupling — the 'rubber doughnut' or Jurid coupling — that perishes and splits with age and heat. Unlike earlier Jaguars where the coupling was a replaceable item, the X150 propshaft was progressively lightened and Jaguar does NOT list the rubber disc as a separate service part, so an official repair requires a complete driveshaft assembly. As the rubber cracks the shaft goes out of balance, producing vibration and eventually a clunk under load; a fully separated coupling can strand the car. Owners and independent Jaguar specialists have successfully cross-referenced/sourced the coupling separately (S-Type/X350 lineage; aftermarket suppliers now stock an X150 Jurid coupling).
before.solution: Inspect the rubber coupling for cracking/splitting at every service. Accepted repairs are fitting a separately-sourced/cross-referenced Jurid coupling (available from independent Jaguar parts specialists) or replacing the complete propshaft assembly. Check and balance the shaft and inspect the center support bearing at the same time.
symptoms: Vibration through the floor that worsens with speed
Clunk or shudder on acceleration or when taking up drive
Visible cracks or splitting in the rubber coupling disc
Driveline rumble at cruise

before.title: Parasitic Battery Drain (Module Not Sleeping / BCM Fault)
before.description: XK owners frequently report flat batteries from parasitic draw when a control module fails to enter sleep mode. Normal quiescent draw should fall to roughly 30-50 mA within about three minutes of lock-up; faulty cars have been measured at 200-220 mA, enough to reach 50% state of charge in under two weeks. The Body Control Module (BCM) is a documented culprit (including cases of burnt board traces/failing capacitors), and the fault is worst on cars driven infrequently.
before.solution: Measure quiescent current after the car has gone to sleep, then use the fuse-pull method (allowing re-sleep between pulls) to isolate the circuit/module. Repair or replace the offending module (commonly the BCM) or the stuck accessory. Keep the car on a smart maintainer if it sits, and verify the battery itself is healthy before chasing the drain.
symptoms: Flat/dead battery after a few days of sitting
Quiescent draw well above ~50 mA
Intermittent electrical gremlins, worse in winter
Modules waking after lock / car not sleeping

before.title: Plastic Crossover / Valley Coolant Pipe Splitting
before.description: The AJ-V8 routes coolant through molded plastic pipes in the engine 'valley'/V (the crossover pipe that plugs into the block, and on 4.2/supercharged cars the valley pipes beneath the supercharger). With age the plastic embrittles and the molded seam splits, or the stubs shear at the block, causing sudden major coolant loss. Because the failure is buried under the intake/supercharger, leaks are hard to spot and can strand the car. Jaguar published a TSB (JTB00566) on coolant leaks from the engine compartment.
before.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system to locate the failed pipe, then replace the crossover/valley pipe(s) — many owners upgrade the 4.2 valley pipes to silicone. Given shared age, it is best practice to renew all accessible plastic cooling pipes and O-rings at once. On supercharged cars the blower must come off, driving labor up.
symptoms: Rapid/major coolant loss with no obvious external leak
Coolant pooling under the car after driving
Low coolant warning and overheating
Steam or coolant smell from engine bay

before.title: Supercharger Nose-Cone Coupler / Isolator Breakdown
before.description: On supercharged XKR models the Eaton supercharger drive uses a plastic coupler/isolator in the nose cone that damps the input drive. The isolator spring breaks and the drive forks wear into the plastic coupling, producing a rattle that steadily worsens. Owners describe a 'bag of marbles' sound from the front of the supercharger snout and a shudder/clonk when shutting the engine off. Jaguar issued a TSB addressing supercharger clatter/knock/rattle on the 5.0L SC engine.
before.solution: Rebuild/refurbish the supercharger nose cone with a new coupler and bearings (rather than replacing the whole blower), or fit an exchange reconditioned supercharger. Confirm the noise is the isolator (not the timing chain or serpentine tensioner) before disassembly. Catching it early prevents metal-to-metal drive fork damage.

before.title: Variable Valve Timing (VVT) Solenoid Cold-Start Rattle
before.description: On the 4.2 AJ-V8, worn VVT solenoids and cam phasers are a leading cause of a brief rattle on cold start-up. The locking pin in the intake-cam actuator sticks or breaks, allowing excessive cam movement (roughly 20 degrees each way) until oil pressure builds. It grows more common at higher mileage and can be aggravated by degraded or wrong-viscosity oil. While often just noise, a failing phaser/solenoid can eventually set cam timing correlation faults.
before.solution: Verify with a scan and by checking cam movement with covers off; test solenoids for proper click/actuation. Replace the affected VVT solenoid(s) and cam phaser hardware, and use fresh oil of the correct grade — some owners find a switch to a quality 5W-40/synthetic reduces the rattle. Full VVT-related repairs can run well over a thousand USD due to access.
symptoms: Rattle/clatter for 1-3 seconds on cold start

proposal.title: Variable Valve Timing (VVT) Solenoid Cold-Start Rattle
proposal.description: On the 4.2 AJ-V8, worn VVT solenoids and cam phasers are a leading cause of a brief rattle on cold start-up. The locking pin in the intake-cam actuator sticks or breaks, allowing excessive cam movement (roughly 20 degrees each way) until oil pressure builds. It grows more common at higher mileage and can be aggravated by degraded or wrong-viscosity oil. While often just noise, a failing phaser/solenoid can eventually set cam timing correlation faults.
proposal.solution: Verify with a scan and by checking cam movement with covers off; test solenoids for proper click/actuation. Replace the affected VVT solenoid(s) and cam phaser hardware, and use fresh oil of the correct grade — some owners find a switch to a quality 5W-40/synthetic reduces the rattle. Full VVT-related repairs can run well over a thousand USD due to access.
symptoms: Rattle/clatter for 1-3 seconds on cold start
Top-of-engine noise that fades as oil pressure builds
Rough idle when cold
Occasional cam-timing fault codes

before.title: ZF 6HP Automatic Transmission Mechatronic Bridge-Seal / Sealing-Sleeve Failure
before.description: The ZF 6HP26 (2006-2009 4.2L cars) and ZF 6HP28 (2009-2014 5.0L cars) automatic used in the X150 XK develops internal hydraulic-pressure loss as the mechatronic unit ages. The 'bridge seal' adapter (the figure-8 sealing sleeve between the valve body/mechatronic and the transmission case) hardens and cracks, and the conductor plate/solenoids degrade, causing loss of line pressure. This is the single most common ZF 6HP fault and owners frequently misdiagnose it as a dead gearbox, replacing the whole unit when only the mechatronic seal or module is at fault. ATF that is never changed (Jaguar marketed it as fill-for-life) accelerates the failure. Well documented across the shared ZF 6HP platform (also used by BMW, Land Rover, Bentley, Maserati).
before.solution: Diagnose with live pressure/adaptation data before condemning the gearbox. In most cases the fix is replacing the mechatronic bridge-seal adapter plus the remaining sleeve/pin seals (sold as a kit) and a full fluid-and-filter (pan) service; more advanced cases need a remanufactured mechatronic/conductor plate. A complete transmission replacement is only warranted if internal clutches are burned.
symptoms: Transmission fault / gearbox warning message (P R N D flashing)
Transmission goes into limp / fail-safe mode
Harsh or banging upshift
Flared / slipping shift
Delayed engagement from Park to Drive or Reverse
Over-revving before the gear engages
